subject: confusion about ggplot and dplyr or others

messages.author: 2cb7822b77eb70b3
messages.subject: confusion about ggplot and dplyr or others
parts:
I am currently using R to manager data and make plots. I am asking for some guidance to learn ggplot, as I just find out ggplot would work better if it is combined with other packages like dplyr or reshape.

Although I know some basic knowledge about the R language, but did not have too much practice. Along this way I am learning R from the online examples, I find a lot of time was wasted. Because there are so many packages available, which can make us worker much more better. If I know the package dplyr or reshape before, I will not waste so much time to learn the others. 

Can anyone give me some suggestions so that I can learn ggplot in the right way? or What kind of knowlege can help me work better if I learn ggplot at the first time?

messages.author: 08f3062efe0fd1ca
messages.subject: Re: confusion about ggplot and dplyr or others
parts:
Hi,

I would recommend you go through the examples at docs.ggplot2.org. Note that data wrangling is now done using package 'tidyr'. In my experience, learning by doing has yielded highest return on an investment.

Cheers,
Roman

messages.author: f4249b01b99d0091
messages.subject: Re: confusion about ggplot and dplyr or others
parts:
I'd add that learning ggplot the 'right' way has nothing per se to do
with knowing how to manipulate data. Yes, ggplot generally is designed
for long data (one observation per row), but you can fully learn the
ggplot system without doing any data reshaping.

That said, I agree with Roman: working through the examples at
ggplot2.org is a good place to start. Then, when you want to apply
your new skills to your own data, you'll recognize how (if) those data
need to be reshaped or summarized.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: confusion about ggplot and dplyr or others
parts:
Hmmm, I'm not sure I agree. Solving many visualisation problems
requires data manipulation, and both data manipulation and data
visualisation are much easier if your data is "tidy"
(http://vita.had.co.nz/papers/tidy-data.html).

Hadley
